--- title: "[EventTime]{.doc-object-name .doc-class .doc-label .doc-label-class}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} A vector of event times that may be exact, or right-, left-, or interval-censored. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_event_time.py#L226-L584){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.CLASS} ```python EventTime() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} `EventTime` is the Python counterpart of etd's `event_time` vector. Create one with `event_time()`, which validates its input, or with `new_event_time()`, which only checks types. Each element has a time and a single-letter status: `"e"` (exact event), `"r"` (right-censored), `"l"` (left-censored), or `"i"` (interval-censored, with an upper bound in `time_max`). Elements print the way etd prints them: `7` for an event, `5+` for right censoring, `3-` for left censoring, and `[2, 4]` for an interval. The vector supports `len()`, indexing with an integer, a slice, an integer array, or a boolean mask (always returning an `EventTime`), and `EventTime.concat()` to combine vectors. Use `extract_time()` and `extract_status()` to get the components back, and `~~greenwood.EventTime.to_frame()` for a table with `time`, `status`{.gd-no-link}, and `time_max` columns. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#fab09133 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw x = gw.event_time( time=[7, 5, 3, 2, None], status=["e", "r", "l", "i", None], time_max=[None, None, None, 4, None], ) x ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 7 5+ 3- [2, 4] ``` ::: ::: Indexing returns another `EventTime`: ::: {#987e5810 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} x[1:4] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 5+ 3- [2, 4] ``` ::: ::: ## Methods {.doc-methods}
Name Description
\__getitem__() Select elements, returning a new event-time vector.
concat() Combine event-time vectors end to end, as `c()` does in R.
format() Format each element as etd does, with `None` for missing elements.
is_na() Return which elements are missing.
to_frame() Split the vector into a table with `"time"`, `"status"`, and `"time_max"` columns.
### [\__getitem__()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Select elements, returning a new event-time vector. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_event_time.py#L300-L365){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python __getitem__(key) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Indexing always returns an `EventTime`, even for a single element, as subsetting an etd vector with `x[i]` does in R. Each element keeps its time, status, and upper bound. Negative integers count from the end, as usual in Python (R's `x[-1]`, which drops an element, has no equivalent here). ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [key]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : An integer, a slice, an array of integer positions, or a boolean mask with one value per element. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [EventTime]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The selected elements. ::: #### Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [IndexError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If an integer position is out of range. [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `key` is not an integer, a slice, an integer array, or a boolean mask. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#1e3f9d85 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw x = gw.event_time( time=[7, 5, 3, 2, None], status=["e", "r", "l", "i", None], time_max=[None, None, None, 4, None], ) x[1:4] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 5+ 3- [2, 4] ``` ::: ::: A boolean mask keeps the elements where it is `True`, here the complete ones: ::: {#20db675e .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} x[~x.is_na()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` 7 5+ 3- [2, 4] ``` ::: ::: ### [concat()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Combine event-time vectors end to end, as `c()` does in R. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_event_time.py#L379-L429){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python concat(items) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The elements of each vector are placed one after another, in the order given. Each keeps its time, status, and upper bound, so vectors with different kinds of censoring can be combined freely. Combining an empty list gives an empty vector. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [items]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Iterable[EventTime]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `EventTime` vectors to combine, in order. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [EventTime]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A vector holding every element of `items`. ::: #### Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If any item is not an `EventTime`. As in R, an event-time vector can't be combined with plain numbers. Build them into an `EventTime` first with `event_time()`. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#c5622216 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw a = gw.event_time(time=[7, 5], status=["e", "r"]) b = gw.event_time(time=[1], status=["i"], time_max=[3]) gw.EventTime.concat([a, b]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` 7 5+ [1, 3] ``` ::: ::: ### [format()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Format each element as etd does, with `None` for missing elements. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_event_time.py#L463-L517){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python format() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} This is the text the vector's printout shows, one string per element, and it matches etd's `format()` character for character. Every number in the vector is formatted together with R's rules: at most 7 significant digits, a shared number of decimal places, and scientific notation when that is narrower. Then each element is marked by its status: - Exact events get a trailing space: `"7 "`. - Right-censored values get a `+`: `"5+"`. - Left-censored values get a `-`: `"3-"`. - Interval-censored values are written as `"[lower, upper]"`. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [list of str or None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : One string per element, or `None` where the element is missing. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#a2f71f72 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw x = gw.event_time(time=[7, 5.5, 3], status=["e", "r", "i"], time_max=[None, None, 4]) x.format() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` ['7.0 ', '5.5+', '[3.0, 4.0]'] ``` ::: ::: Very different magnitudes share one layout, switching to scientific notation as R does: ::: {#e10e4148 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} gw.event_time(time=[0.001234, 12345.6, 7], status=["e", "r", "l"]).format() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=7} ``` ['1.23400e-03 ', '1.23456e+04+', '7.00000e+00-'] ``` ::: ::: ### [is_na()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Return which elements are missing. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_event_time.py#L433-L461){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python is_na() ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} An element is missing when any of its times is missing (`nan`), as in etd's `is.na()`. For an interval-censored element that includes a missing upper bound. A missing status alone only occurs together with a missing time, because `event_time()` rejects a missing status where the time is present. Estimators drop missing elements when fitting. ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [numpy.ndarray]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A boolean array with one value per element, `True` where the element is missing. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#b937eba2 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw x = gw.event_time(time=[7, None, 2], status=["e", None, "i"], time_max=[None, None, 4]) x.is_na() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=8} ``` array([False, True, False]) ``` ::: ::: Select the complete elements with the inverted mask: ::: {#f143f512 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} x[~x.is_na()] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=9} ``` 7 [2, 4] ``` ::: ::: ### [to_frame()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method} ::: {.doc-subject} Split the vector into a table with `"time"`, `"status"`, and `"time_max"` columns. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/main/greenwood/_event_time.py#L539-L584){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python to_frame(*, format=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} This is the counterpart of etd's `as_tibble()`: the reverse of `event_time()`, with one row per element. The `"time_max"` column is always included, and is missing for elements that are not interval-censored. Missing values are nulls. Use the table to inspect a vector, to join it back onto other data, or to export it. ::: #### Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [format]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Output format: `None` (default), `"pandas"`, `"polars"`, or `"pyarrow"`. When `None`, a backend is auto-detected (Polars, then Pandas, then PyArrow). ::: #### Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [pandas.DataFrame, polars.DataFrame, or pyarrow.Table]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : One row per element, with the columns `"time"`, `"status"`, and `"time_max"`. ::: #### Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ImportError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the requested DataFrame library (or, with `format=None`, any of them) is not installed. ::: #### Examples {.doc-examples} ::: {#da82a7b5 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw x = gw.event_time(time=[7, 5, 2], status=["e", "r", "i"], time_max=[None, None, 4]) x.to_frame(format="polars") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=10} ```{=html}
shape: (3, 3)
timestatustime_max
f64strf64
7.0"e"null
5.0"r"null
2.0"i"4.0
``` ::: :::
